findings.description: The new memo helper `_lc_chunk_tok` indexes the bash indexed array `_lc_tok` with its second argument twice: `[[ -n "${_lc_tok[$2]:-}" ]]` and `_lc_tok[$2]=...`. Bash evaluates an indexed-array subscript as an arithmetic expression and performs a second round of expansion on it, so a subscript of the form `x[$(cmd)]` runs `cmd`. The value passed is `chunk_idx` from the manifest, which is parsed with `IFS=$'\t' read -r priority filepath chunk_idx` over lines written as `pri<TAB>filepath<TAB>idx`. `filepath` is the capture of `^diff --git a/(.+) b/` over the untrusted diff, so a header such as `diff --git a/x<TAB>q[$(id>/tmp/p)] b/x` yields `chunk_idx='q[$(id>/tmp/p)]<TAB>0'`. The two pre-scans skip such rows because they test `-f "$temp_dir/chunk_${c_idx}"` first, but the main include loop only tests `-n` before calling `cat` and then `_lc_chunk_tok`. Callers capture `prepare_content` via `$(...)`; without `shopt -s inherit_errexit` errexit is off inside the substitution, so the failed `cat` does not abort and the subscript is evaluated with the attacker string. The only thing currently blocking the trigger is that git C-quotes tabs in diff headers (`"a/x\tq"`), which is incidental: any caller that feeds a hand-built or API-assembled diff, or a reviewer given a `.patch` file, removes that barrier and this becomes remote command execution in the review environment (which holds model API keys and git credentials).
findings.failure_mode: A PR or patch whose diff header path contains a raw tab followed by `name[$(command)]` causes arbitrary command execution in the reviewing process when the diff exceeds the token budget. With git-quoted input the same malformed row instead aborts or mis-parses the manifest, folding that file into a neighbouring chunk and silently removing it from per-file prioritisation.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the index the field that can never absorb a tab: write the manifest as `pri<TAB>idx<TAB>filepath` and read it as `read -r priority chunk_idx filepath` so the path is the remainder. In addition, guard the sink: at the top of `_lc_chunk_tok` require `[[ "$2" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 1`, and in the main include loop add the same `-f "$temp_dir/chunk_${chunk_idx}"` test the two pre-scans already use before `cat`/`_lc_chunk_tok`. Optionally reject or quote any captured path containing a tab at parse time and log it.

findings.trigger_anchor: unset GIT_DIR GIT_WORK_TREE GIT_INDEX_FILE GIT_COMMON_DIR GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES GIT_DISCOVERY_ACROSS_FILESYSTEM
findings.description: `_vd_committed` runs `git ls-files` and `git diff --quiet HEAD` inside the directory of the dissent envelope (`--envelope` or the sibling of `--file`). Before doing so it unsets not only the variables that redirect the repository (GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, GIT_INDEX_FILE, GIT_COMMON_DIR, object dirs, namespace) but also the two that bound repository discovery, `GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES` and `GIT_DISCOVERY_ACROSS_FILESYSTEM`, and, via `$(git rev-parse --local-env-vars)`, `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS`/`GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, which is how a parent process passes protective config such as `safe.directory` or `core.fsmonitor=false`. Git then walks up from an arbitrary caller-supplied directory to whatever `.git` it finds and honours that repository's `.git/config` (core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath, core.pager, diff.external all execute commands). In a CI runner where scratch directories live under an untrusted checkout, or where the operator deliberately set a ceiling to stop exactly this walk, the script removes that control for a check whose only purpose is to decide whether a sidecar's rows are 'history'.
findings.failure_mode: A verdict check pointed (by `--envelope`, or by placing the feedback file) at a directory beneath a repository with hostile or unexpected config runs that repository's configured commands during `git ls-files`/`git diff`, and a caller-set discovery ceiling or `-c` safety config is silently discarded.
findings.suggested_fix: Unset only the variables that name a repository (GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, GIT_INDEX_FILE, GIT_COMMON_DIR, GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY, GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES, GIT_NAMESPACE, GIT_IMPLICIT_WORK_TREE); keep GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES, GIT_DISCOVERY_ACROSS_FILESYSTEM and GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS/GIT_CONFIG_COUNT intact. Pass `-c core.fsmonitor=false -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null -c core.pager=cat -c diff.external=` on the two git calls so repository config cannot execute commands, and consider verifying `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` is an ancestor of the envelope directory the caller expects before trusting the 'committed' answer.

findings.description: The new default plans a second dissent chain from the OTHER provider family, and the comment states that credential presence alone decides where that chain starts and that 'an absent key is true: a config that predates the key runs two voices'. Once flatline_protocol.*.enabled is true, the set of third-party LLM vendors that receive the full `main...HEAD` diff is therefore determined by which API keys happen to exist in the environment, not by an explicit opt-in in config. An operator who adds ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY to CI for unrelated tooling silently starts shipping source diffs (including any fixtures, .env samples, or embedded secrets in the change set) to that vendor on every /review-sprint and /audit-sprint.
findings.failure_mode: Silent expansion of data egress to an additional external LLM provider with no config change and no explicit approval; proprietary or regulated code leaves the trust boundary and the operator believes only the configured `model` vendor receives it.
findings.suggested_fix: Default `companion_voice` to false in the example, or require the companion provider to be named explicitly in config (e.g. `companion_voice: { enabled: true, provider: anthropic }`) rather than inferred from env key presence. Record the resolved destination providers in the adversarial-review envelope and print them at dispatch so the egress is auditable.

findings.anchor: .loa.config.yaml.example: `budget_cents: 150            # Gate on ONE dissent call's pre-dispatch cost estimate` (code_review block)
findings.description: The diff documents that `budget_cents` gates only a single pre-dispatch estimate and explicitly does NOT count: fallback hops, the companion voice, or KF-004 repairs (up to 5 findings per voice, each up to 3 repair-chain hops). Worst case per run is roughly 2 voices x (primary + fallback hops + 15 repair calls), none of which are cost-gated. The only remaining bound is wall clock (5 x timeout x 2 = 600 s per voice at defaults), and the LOA_ADVERSARIAL_REPAIR_BUDGET_SECONDS pin is floored at 'two of the heaviest hop's charges plus a timeout', so it cannot be tightened below that. Because the reviewed diff is untrusted PR content fed verbatim to the dissenter, prompt injection in the diff can steer the model into emitting deliberately malformed findings to trigger the maximum repair rounds.
findings.failure_mode: Token-spend amplification / cost DoS by any PR author: a single review can consume 20-30x the amount the operator believes `budget_cents` caps, across two paid vendors, while the config field name implies a spend ceiling.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an aggregate per-run ceiling (e.g. `max_run_cents`) accumulated across voices, fallback hops and repair calls, failing closed with status budget_exceeded once the running total plus the next call's estimate would exceed it. Rename or alias the existing field to `estimate_gate_cents` so the semantics are not misread, and cap repair calls per run (not just per voice).

findings.anchor: .loa.config.yaml.example: comment `Credential presence only decides where the companion chain starts (no key → the CLI hop)` and default chains `[gpt-5.5, codex-headless]` / `[opus, claude-headless]`
findings.cross_file_justification: The CLI hop is dispatched by .claude/scripts/adversarial-review.sh (allowed in .claude/skills/auditing-security/SKILL.md allowed-tools as `Bash(.claude/scripts/adversarial-review.sh *)`). That script is not in the diff and could not be read here, so the invocation flags and permission mode of the headless CLI are unverified. The diff is the trigger because it makes the CLI hop a default-planned step whenever the other family's key is absent, which is the common CI state.
findings.description: With `companion_voice: true` and no API key for the other family, the default chain falls through to a headless CLI agent (`claude-headless` or `codex-headless`) resolved from PATH, and the untrusted `main...HEAD` diff is handed to it as the prompt. Two risks follow. (1) If the headless CLI is launched with any tool/write permission, prompt injection embedded in the PR diff can drive it to execute actions in the reviewer's checkout or CI runner. (2) The binary is located by PATH lookup ('plan the CLI hop when its binary is on PATH'); a PATH that includes a writable or repo-relative directory lets a PR plant a fake `claude`/`codex` executable that runs with the reviewer's credentials.
findings.failure_mode: Untrusted PR content reaches a locally executing agent; worst case is arbitrary command execution on the review host or exfiltration of the API keys present in its environment. Severity is MEDIUM pending verification of how adversarial-review.sh invokes the CLI.
findings.suggested_fix: In adversarial-review.sh, invoke the headless CLI with an explicit read-only/no-tools permission profile and a hard output-only contract, resolve the binary to an absolute path once and verify it is not under the repository or a world-writable directory, and consider defaulting the CLI hop to off (API key required) for the security_audit block.

findings.anchor: .loa.config.yaml.example: commented block `# companion_chain:` / `#   anthropic: [opus, claude-headless]` / `#   openai: [gpt-5.5, codex-headless]`
findings.cross_file_justification: Hop-name resolution happens in .claude/scripts/adversarial-review.sh, which is not in the diff; the comment 'used as given — no PATH filter' describes behaviour that bypasses the default chain's validation and so needs the script to enforce an allowlist.
findings.description: The override is documented as 'used as given — no PATH filter: a CLI hop named here is planned even when its binary is absent, and fails as that hop'. That means hop names from .loa.config.yaml are accepted without being checked against the model catalog or the set of known CLI hops. When the reviewer runs against a PR branch that carries its own .loa.config.yaml, the config is attacker-influenced; if any hop name is ever mapped to an executable name or interpolated into a command, this becomes a repo-controlled command surface. The comment also notes a hop that duplicates the primary fallback_chain 'stays in the chain', so a misconfiguration can silently remove the independence the second voice is supposed to provide while still reporting voices_planned 2.
findings.failure_mode: Unknown or malicious hop names are accepted at plan time and only fail at dispatch; independence of the second voice can be defeated by configuration while the envelope still looks two-voice until `companion_voice.independent` is inspected.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate every companion_chain entry at config load against the catalog plus the fixed CLI-hop enum and refuse unknown names (exit non-zero, not 'fail as that hop'). Reject or warn loudly when a companion hop shares a family or model with the primary fallback_chain rather than listing it under shared_hops.

findings.anchor: .loa.config.yaml.example: `companion_voice: true        # ... with no route to the other family every audit is DEGRADED_SECURITY_REVIEW; false where one voice is the host's shape` (security_audit block)
findings.description: The DEGRADED_SECURITY_REVIEW marker is only emitted when the companion voice is enabled but unreachable. The example config explicitly tells operators to set `companion_voice: false` to make the marker go away. A single-voice audit by configuration therefore carries no degradation signal at all, even though it provides exactly the same (reduced) assurance as the degraded case. The marker is a control that can be silenced by disabling the control it reports on.
findings.failure_mode: Downstream consumers of adversarial-audit.json (verdict-derive.sh, COMPLETED gate, humans) cannot distinguish a deliberately single-voice security audit from a two-voice one unless they inspect voices_planned; the degradation signal is trivially suppressible.
findings.suggested_fix: Always record `voices_planned` and a `single_voice_reason` (configured | no_route | duplicate_voice) in the envelope and have the audit template surface it in the report header. Consider emitting a weaker SINGLE_VOICE_SECURITY_REVIEW marker when companion_voice is false so the reduced assurance is visible without being treated as an error.

findings.anchor: .claude/data/skill-includes/input_guardrails.md: `| Script missing, non-zero exit, or unparseable output | Continue (fail-open) |`
findings.cross_file_justification: The guardrails orchestrator is the only pre-dispatch input check in front of the dissent calls; the diff doubles the number of external LLM dispatches (two voices) and adds CLI-hop dispatch that this fail-open gate fronts, so its failure behaviour matters more after this change.
findings.description: The mechanized pre-execution guardrail continues on a missing script, a non-zero exit, or unparseable output. For an auditing skill whose downstream step now sends the invocation input and diff to up to two external providers and possibly a local headless agent, a crashed or deleted guardrails-orchestrator.sh removes the only input screen with no error surfaced to the operator.
findings.failure_mode: An attacker who can break or remove the guardrails script (or trigger a parse error in it) disables input screening silently; the review proceeds and dispatches to external LLMs as if the check had passed.
findings.suggested_fix: Fail closed for the security_audit skill (HALT on missing script or non-zero exit) or at minimum WARN visibly and record `guardrails: skipped` in the envelope so the degraded state is auditable. Keep fail-open, if desired, only for non-security skills.

findings.description: The scratch-repository helper passes `-c protocol.file.allow=always` to every git invocation. This switches off the file-transport restriction Git added for CVE-2022-39253 (submodule clones from local paths). In the shown hunks the helper is only defined, so it is not yet clear which fixtures depend on it; if any fixture ever clones or updates a submodule from a path it did not create itself, the protection is gone for that operation.
findings.failure_mode: A fixture that clones a repository containing a .gitmodules pointing at a local path would follow it, which the default `protocol.file.allow=user` would refuse.
findings.suggested_fix: Drop the override unless a specific fixture needs it; if one does, pass it only on that call rather than in the shared wrapper, and add a comment naming the fixture.

findings.description: Ownership of a leftover `sprint-comp-<n>` directory is proven by a marker file `.sprint-comp-<n>.owner` in the shared a2a directory inside the checkout. Any local writer of that directory can create such a marker with a `where` line copied from this host and a dead pid, and the next teardown will recursively delete `grimoires/loa/a2a/sprint-comp-<n>` and any `.reap-*` siblings. The naming convention makes a real sprint collision unlikely, and the deletion requires write access the attacker already holds, so impact is confined to confusing or destroying test artefacts.
findings.failure_mode: A planted marker causes the suite's teardown to delete a directory it did not create.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the owner's start token (already computed by _sweep_start) in the marker and require it to match the dead pid's recorded token, or restrict the sweep to directories whose inode was recorded in the marker at setup.

findings.description: The `errlog` stub arm emits `sk-ant-api03-SECRETSECRETSECRETSECRET1234`, a string in the real Anthropic key format, and CMP-13 exports `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-presence-only-never-printed` without the leak assertions that CMP-4 and CMP-6 apply. Both values are obvious canaries, but the committed key-shaped literal is the kind of string that repository secret scanners flag, and CMP-13 leaves one credential path unasserted.
findings.failure_mode: Secret-scanning tooling raises a false positive on the committed fixture; a regression that prints the key in the CMP-13 path would go unnoticed because that test does not check stdout or stderr for the canary.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the key-shaped canary (it is needed to exercise the mask) but build it at runtime from parts, and add the same `[[ "$result" != *canary* ]]` and stderr assertions to CMP-13 that CMP-6 already has.

findings.anchor: @test "CMP-93 the run lock fails open on a lock directory that is not ours, and on no hash tool
findings.cross_file_justification: The test pins the behavior of _adv_take_run_lock in the production adversarial-review script ($ADVERSARIAL_REVIEW): when the per-user lock directory is a symlink or not owned by the invoking user, or when neither sha256sum nor shasum exists, the run proceeds with _ADV_RUN_LOCK_DIR empty and only a single stderr warning.
findings.description: The run lock is the only guard around the envelope move-aside (.prev) and rewrite sequence pinned by CMP-64/CMP-69. CMP-93 asserts that an unusable lock directory (symlink, wrong owner) plus an unavailable XDG_CACHE_HOME fallback results in fail-open: the review runs unguarded. Refusing to follow the symlink is correct, but on a shared host where the primary lock directory sits under a world-writable tmp, a local user can plant that symlink to switch off mutual exclusion for the victim's runs.
findings.failure_mode: Two concurrent runs against the same output directory interleave move-aside and write. The final adversarial-review.json or its rejected sidecar can belong to the wrong round or be torn, and verdict-derive.sh (exercised in CMP-64) consumes it as authoritative.
findings.suggested_fix: Fail closed when both the primary lock directory and the XDG_CACHE_HOME fallback are unusable, or add a last-resort private directory under $HOME (mode 700, ownership-checked). If fail-open must remain, gate it behind an explicit opt-in such as LOA_ADVERSARIAL_LOCK_OPTIONAL=1 and keep the warning.

findings.anchor: @test "CMP-82 the reaper KILLs a pid only while it is still the process it collected
findings.cross_file_justification: CMP-82 pins that _adv_kill_same with an empty token signals the bare pid, and CMP-71 pins that an unreadable start token at fork keeps the companion tracked by pid alone. Both describe the reaper in the production script.
findings.description: The reaper's pid-reuse defense (start-time token compare, pinned by CMP-62/CMP-100/CMP-109) is bypassed whenever a token could not be read: the fallback is to TERM and then KILL the bare pid. For the direct child this is safe because the pid cannot be recycled before wait. For collected tree descendants it is not: a descendant whose /proc/<pid>/stat read failed during the frozen collection is later signalled by number alone, after a grace window that can follow a wait of up to the global ceiling (~1000 s per CMP-65).
findings.failure_mode: On a busy host a recycled pid belonging to an unrelated same-user process receives SIGTERM and SIGKILL from the reaper.
findings.suggested_fix: When the frozen-collection token read fails, retry via the ps lstart fallback (_adv_lstart_token, CMP-97) before recording the pid, and if still no token is available, restrict the fallback to the direct child only and skip signalling untokenised descendants after the grace window.

findings.anchor: @test "CMP-99 the fold survives its redactor under errexit and pipefail
findings.cross_file_justification: The tests drive production helpers by setting _ADV_REDACTOR_BIN and _ADV_FLOCK_BIN as variables visible to the sourced script, which indicates the script resolves these binaries from an overridable variable rather than a fixed path.
findings.description: The redactor is the control that keeps raw companion log lines (which can carry provider error bodies, paths, or tokens) out of stderr and envelopes; CMP-99 shows the fold pipes the diagnostic through whatever _ADV_REDACTOR_BIN names. If the production script initialises these with an environment default (for example ${_ADV_REDACTOR_BIN:-...}), any caller or CI step that can set environment variables can replace the redactor with cat, or point _ADV_FLOCK_BIN at a script that always succeeds and silently disables the per-key takeover section. Verify how the script initialises these variables; if they are assigned unconditionally inside the script this finding does not apply.
findings.failure_mode: Unredacted companion diagnostics reach stderr and logs, or the lock takeover runs without its flock, through nothing more than an environment variable.
findings.suggested_fix: Assign the helper paths unconditionally in the script and expose a test seam only when an explicit test-mode variable is set (for example LOA_ADVERSARIAL_TEST_HOOKS=1 and a check that BATS_TEST_FILENAME is non-empty). Alternatively, resolve the redactor relative to the script directory and ignore external overrides.

findings.anchor: @test "CMP-186 --diff-range's diff reads no system-wide gitattributes — GIT_ATTR_NOSYSTEM reaches git — while the repository's own .git/info/attributes still applies
findings.trigger_anchor: @test "CMP-186 --diff-range's diff reads no system-wide gitattributes — GIT_ATTR_NOSYSTEM reaches git — while the repository's own .git/info/attributes still applies
findings.cross_file_justification: The behaviour under test is _adv_range_diff in .claude/scripts/adversarial-review.sh. CMP-164 and CMP-180 in this same diff pin that every other local, uncommitted diff-shaping source (diff.* config, core.attributesFile, diff.ignoreSubmodules, committed and worktree .gitattributes via the empty-tree attr source) is neutralised so 'the operator's config never hides what the range changed'. CMP-186 pins the one exception.
findings.description: CMP-186's second half asserts that a `*.txt -diff` line in `.git/info/attributes` turns the reviewed range diff into `Binary files ... differ`, and fixes this as the intended contract. Every other local source that could shape or hide the diff is deliberately ignored by the sibling tests, because the adversarial reviewer must see what the range actually changed. `.git/info/attributes` sits in the same local-only `.git/` directory as `.git/config`, is written by the same actor working in the checkout, and is the only attribute source left after GIT_ATTR_NOSYSTEM and the empty-tree attr source. A single `* -diff` line there blinds both the primary and the companion to every text change while the run still finishes as `reviewed` with a `metadata.model`, which is exactly what the COMPLETED gate checks (CMP-182).
findings.failure_mode: An agent, or prompt-injected code run during the sprint, writes `* -diff` to `.git/info/attributes`. The reviewed diff contains only binary markers, both voices return zero findings, the envelope is written as `reviewed`, and the adversarial-review gate opens on code nobody reviewed.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat `.git/info/attributes` like the other local sources. Either pass `--text` to the range diff so `-diff` attributes cannot hide hunks, or detect `Binary files` lines whose blobs `git diff --numstat` reports as text and refuse the run with its own status. Then flip the second half of CMP-186 to assert the `+b` hunk is still shown under `.git/info/attributes`.

findings.anchor: @test "CMP-170 both resources say a --record-fallback record never opens the COMPLETED gate, with its remedy; both skills allowlist the br and log-discovered-issue steps they prescribe, narrowly
findings.trigger_anchor: grep -q 'LOA_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEW_ENFORCE=false' "$r" || { echo "$s: no remedy named"; return 1; }
findings.cross_file_justification: The files the test constrains are the agent-facing .claude/skills/{reviewing-code,auditing-security}/resources/ADVERSARIAL-REVIEW.md. The gate they describe is .claude/hooks/safety/adversarial-review-gate.sh (asserted by CMP-182 in this diff).
findings.description: CMP-170 requires both agent-facing skill resources to contain the literal `LOA_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEW_ENFORCE=false` as the remedy when a fallback record leaves the COMPLETED gate closed. The gate exists to stop the agent from marking a sprint complete without an independent review. Documenting the enforcement-off switch in the instructions the constrained party reads reduces the gate to an advisory control. Whether the hook reads that variable from an environment the agent can influence (a project .env, settings, or an exported shell variable) is not verifiable from this diff, so the reach of the bypass is uncertain, but the test guarantees the instruction is present.
findings.failure_mode: A review fails, the agent records a fallback, the gate stays closed, and the agent follows the documented remedy and disables enforcement. The sprint completes with no adversarial review and no record that enforcement was switched off.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the operator switch out of agent-facing resources and prescribe STOP-and-escalate, as CMP-182 already requires of Phase 0. If the switch must be named, mark it operator-only and have the gate hook write an audit row whenever it honours the variable. Change CMP-170 to assert the escalation text rather than the env-var literal.

findings.anchor: @test "CMP-171 the kept-workdir sweep in TMPDIR never follows nor fails on a symlink at a workdir path — the suite's one link rule
findings.description: The test creates a symlink at a predictable name under the shared `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}`; the sprint id embeds only the pid. The `[[ -L "$lnk" ]]` check followed by `ln -s` is a time-of-check/time-of-use window in a world-writable directory, so another local user can pre-place a directory or link at that path. The no-follow teardown being tested bounds the damage to a spurious failure or a link dropped inside a foreign directory, but the suite deliberately writes to a shared path it does not own.
findings.failure_mode: A local user pre-creates `/tmp/adversarial-sprint-comp-<pid>-lnk171` as a directory. `ln -s` places the link inside it, teardown sweeps a path the test did not create, and the trailing `rm -f -- "$lnk"` leaves the link behind.
findings.suggested_fix: Point TMPDIR for the teardown call at a private `mktemp -d` under `$T` so the sweep runs against a directory only this test owns, or use an unpredictable `mktemp -u` name and assert `ln -s` succeeded before invoking teardown.

findings.cross_file_justification: NRM-19 in the diff-touched test file pins the no-digest fallback of `_adv_run_tag` in .claude/scripts/adversarial-review.sh. The test asserts the truncated shape rather than distinctness, so the collision in the production function is locked in by this suite.
findings.description: When neither sha256sum nor shasum is on PATH, the run-tag fallback hex-encodes the raw tag, cuts the hex at 200 characters (the first 100 raw bytes), and appends only the byte length. Two invalid tags longer than 100 bytes that share their first 100 bytes and their total length therefore map to one sidecar filename. That is the exact outcome the tag scheme exists to prevent (the suite's own headline is that `c.1` and `c1` never share a sidecar). NRM-19 asserts the truncated form and only checks distinctness for tags that differ inside the first 100 bytes.
findings.failure_mode: Two runs with long, prefix-sharing tags on a host without a digest tool append to the same `adversarial-rejected-<type>-h....jsonl`, interleaving rows and attributing one run's rejected payloads to the other in `metadata.rejected_sidecar`.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the whole tag in the name derivation: for example hex of the first 60 bytes plus hex of the last 40 bytes plus the length, or use POSIX `cksum` (always present) over the raw tag as the no-sha fallback. Add an NRM-19 assertion that two 150-byte tags differing only in their last byte produce different names.

findings.description: The credential scrub consumes only the first line of `_adv_cred_aliases` output (`read -ra row <<<"$(...)"`) and then calls `unset "$v"` with no `-v` and no option terminator. NRM-8 reads the same table with unquoted word splitting, which tolerates both space- and newline-separated output; the scrub does not. If the table ever emits one alias per line, every alias after the first stays set, and the function reports success. A token beginning with `-` would be parsed by `unset` as an option rather than a name.
findings.failure_mode: An operator's real provider key survives setup's scrub, is inherited by every `bash -c` child the suite spawns, and silently flips the routing assertions in NRM-6 and NRM-20 (tiny vs claude-headless) so the suite exercises a different hop than it claims to.
findings.suggested_fix: Read all tokens regardless of separator, validate each as a shell identifier, and unset by name explicitly: `mapfile -t row < <(_adv_cred_aliases "$p" | tr ' ' '\n' | sed '/^$/d')`, then `[[ "$v" =~ ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$ ]] || return 1; unset -v "$v"`.

findings.anchor: @test "NRM-45 a rejected_summary row is a bounded, typed surface
findings.cross_file_justification: NRM-45 and NRM-48 in tests/unit/adversarial-review-normalise.bats pin the sanitiser that process_findings in .claude/scripts/adversarial-review.sh applies to rejected_summary rows and reject-reason log lines. The pinned contract is exactly the jq class [\u0000-\u001f\u007f] plus an LC_ALL=C grep of the same bytes, so the production clean is bounded to C0 and DEL by test.
findings.description: The 'control-free' guarantee for the model-written title, anchor, description_head, severity and reason fields covers only C0 controls and DEL. C1 controls U+0080 to U+009F, the line and paragraph separators U+2028/U+2029, bidi overrides U+202A to U+202E and U+2066 to U+2069, and zero-width characters are neither stripped nor tested. The tests themselves name the threat as terminal and markdown injection ('## Injected', ESC, BEL fixtures). xterm-family terminals interpret UTF-8 encoded C1 as controls (U+009B is CSI), and bidi overrides reorder displayed text, so the gap leaves that threat partly open for model output that reaches the operator's stderr or a rendered report.
findings.failure_mode: A model finding whose severity or title contains U+009B followed by an SGR sequence, or a U+202E override, passes the clean unchanged. When the reject reason or summary row is printed to the terminal or rendered into the report, the visible line is recoloured, overwritten or reversed, so the rejected finding's real content is disguised in operator-facing output.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the clean to the full set of non-printing code points, for example reject or space-replace [\u0000-\u001f\u007f-\u009f​-‏ -‮⁠-⁤⁦-⁩﻿], applied via explode/map/implode so it is still linear time per NRM-49. Pin it by adding fixtures to NRM-45 and NRM-48 containing U+009B, U+2028 and U+202E and asserting they do not survive in title, severity, reason, anchor or description_head.

findings.anchor: @test "NRM-28 the test seams are honoured under the bats marker only
findings.cross_file_justification: NRM-28 and NRM-25 pin load-time behaviour of .claude/scripts/adversarial-review.sh: with BATS_TEST_FILENAME or BATS_VERSION present in the environment, the script keeps _ADV_FLOCK_BIN, _ADV_PGREP_BIN, _ADV_LOCK_WAIT_CLI and honours LOA_ADVERSARIAL_NO_FM_DERIVATION; without the marker it drops them.
findings.description: The test seams are gated solely on two ordinary, inheritable environment variables that bats exports. Any invocation of the real script from inside another bats process (an integration suite, a CI step that runs bats, or a shell where BATS_VERSION leaked) silently re-enables them. In that state the environment chooses which binary the script executes in place of flock and pgrep, can disable the CLI lock wait, and can turn off failure_mode derivation so findings pass without that field. The marginal risk over plain PATH control is small, which is why this is a hardening item rather than an exploitable gap.
findings.failure_mode: A CI job runs the adversarial review from a bats-driven integration test with BATS_VERSION set. A compromised or misconfigured environment also sets _ADV_FLOCK_BIN to an attacker-controlled path; the review executes that binary with the operator's credentials while believing it is serialising CLI hops, or sets LOA_ADVERSARIAL_NO_FM_DERIVATION=1 and the review emits findings that lack failure_mode.
findings.suggested_fix: Require an explicit opt-in such as LOA_ADVERSARIAL_TEST_SEAMS=1 in addition to the bats marker, and constrain _ADV_*_BIN to an absolute, executable path under the repository's tests/ tree or owned by the current uid. Add a negative case to NRM-28 where BATS_VERSION is set but the opt-in is absent and assert the seams are dropped.

findings.anchor: @test "NRM-46 no payload-sized value reaches jq on argv
findings.description: The NRM-46 Python lint is the control that keeps model payloads off jq's argv, preventing the E2BIG and truncation failures NRM-43 and NRM-46 were written for. It is regex based with bypasses a later edit would slip through: (a) a quoted flag, kv+=("--arg" "$name" "$payload"), does not match because the regex requires whitespace immediately after --arg; (b) a flag held in a variable, "$flag" x "$payload", is invisible; (c) the trailing-comment strip re.split(r'\s{2,}# ', line) is applied before quote parsing, so a quoted operand containing two spaces and '# ' hides every operand after it; (d) the SMALL allowlist is by name only, and names such as last_error, reject_reason, sidecar_reject_reason, why, _ff_why, violated_clause, _enforced_err, _vq_err and stop_reason carry model- or provider-derived text whose caps the lint never verifies. The lint's own fixture self-tests exercise none of (a) to (c).
findings.failure_mode: A refactor passes a finding through one of these forms, the lint passes, and a model finding above 128 KiB makes jq exit with E2BIG mid-run or silently truncates the field, reintroducing the review-wide failure the suite guards against.
findings.suggested_fix: Add fixtures for (a), (b) and (c) to the lint's self-test and widen the flag match to ["']?--(?:argjson|arg)["']?\s+, stripping comments only outside quoted spans. For (d), either assert in the suite that each allowlisted reason or error variable is produced by a capping helper such as _adv_error_summary, or remove them from SMALL and route them through _adv_jq_pair or a file.

findings.description: `_vd_fifo_watchdog` validates its deadline (`VD_FIFO_DEADLINE` must match `^[1-9][0-9]*$`) but never validates the `reader` PID it is handed. `_vd_tree "$reader"` echoes the argument back unchanged, so an empty, `0`, or negative value flows straight into `kill -TERM $t` and `kill -KILL $t ...`. `kill -KILL 0` kills the whole process group (the entire bats run); `kill -KILL -1` kills every process the user can signal. The function also snapshots the tree into `$t`, sleeps one second, then re-sends SIGKILL to the stale `$t` list alongside a fresh snapshot; any PID in `$t` that exited and was recycled during that second now belongs to an unrelated process. The helper runs detached in the background with the test's privileges. No caller is visible in the shown hunk parts (1-4 of 8), so it is either dead code or invoked from the unshown remainder.
findings.failure_mode: A caller passing a stale or unset `$!` (e.g. the reader's `&` did not execute and `$!` still names an earlier background job such as the watchdog's own `sleep`), or an empty variable, makes the watchdog SIGKILL the wrong process tree: the bats runner itself, a sibling CI job owned by the same user, or an arbitrary recycled PID. On a shared CI runner this is a denial of service against other jobs and loses the test report.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate `reader` with the same regex used for `dl` (`[[ "$reader" =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || return 1`) and refuse `1`, `$$`, `$PPID`, and `$BATS_ROOT_PID`-style ancestors. Drop the stale `$t` from the final `kill -KILL` and re-derive the tree only. Better: start the reader in its own process group (`setsid`) and kill the group with `kill -- -"$pgid"`, which has no recycling window. If no test in this file calls the helper, remove it.

findings.description: The `_vd_git` isolation is incomplete and the comment overstates it. The `$(command git rev-parse --local-env-vars)` substitution is expanded as an argument of `unset`, so that git invocation runs under the caller's unscrubbed environment before anything is removed (benign for `--local-env-vars`, but the opposite order from what the comment describes). Variables outside git's local-repo list survive into `git init`/`add`/`commit`: `GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR` (hooks copied into the fixture repo on `init` and executed on `commit`), `GIT_EXEC_PATH` (alternate `git-*` binaries), `GIT_EDITOR`/`GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR`, and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` (`git/ignore` and `git/attributes` still load even with `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null`). If `rev-parse --local-env-vars` fails, the hardcoded fallback omits `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS` and `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, which a hook environment carries whenever the outer git was invoked with `-c`, and which can inject `core.hooksPath` or `core.fsmonitor`. Like the watchdog, no caller appears in the visible hunk parts.
findings.failure_mode: A test run from inside a git hook or from a dotfiles shell with `GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR` or `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS` set produces fixture commits that execute the caller's hooks or config-selected commands, or an `add -A` that silently drops fixture files via a user ignore file, yielding fixture state the test did not write. The attacker must already control the shell environment, so this is hardening rather than a trust boundary.
findings.suggested_fix: Run fixture git under an allowlisted environment: `env -i PATH="$PATH" HOME=/nonexistent GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1 GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR=/nonexistent git -C "$1" -c user.email=t@t -c user.name=t "${@:2}"`, or at minimum also unset `GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR GIT_EXEC_PATH XDG_CONFIG_HOME GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` and pass `--template=` to `init`. Remove the helper if the remaining hunk parts do not use it.

findings.trigger_anchor: _vd_shsrc() {  # <file> → the lines that hand a shell an interpolated program
findings.description: The _vd_shsrc lint exists to stop suite code from re-parsing a tmpdir path as shell source (the suite deliberately uses a directory named with a double quote, a dollar sign and backticks). Its regex only recognises `sh`/`bash` followed by a `-c` flag group and then a quote or line continuation. It does not match: other shells (`zsh -c`, `dash -c`, `ksh -c`, `"$SHELL" -c`), `bash -c -- "x $d"` (the `--` is not `-[A-Za-z]+`), an unquoted program (`bash -c $prog` / `bash -c x$d`), an expansion after the closing quote (`bash -c "x"$d` — the first grep cannot cross the closing double quote and the second requires a single quote), or a program fed on stdin or via process substitution (`bash -s <<EOF … $d`, `bash <<<"x $d"`, `bash <(printf … "$d")`, `source "$d/x"`). A future test written in any of these forms would reintroduce the exact injection class the lint guards against and still pass the suite.
findings.failure_mode: A test author writes `run zsh -c "cd $d && …"` or `bash -c "x"$d`; the lint reports nothing, and a tmpdir or checkout path containing shell metacharacters is executed as code when the suite runs.
findings.suggested_fix: Broaden the shell matcher to `(ba|da|z|k|a)?sh|\$\{?SHELL` and accept `--` in the flag run; add a pattern for an unquoted or post-quote expansion (`-c[[:space:]]+[^'"[:space:]]*\$` and `-c[[:space:]]+"[^"]*"\$`); add patterns for `bash -s`, `<<<`, `<(`, and `source`/`.` with an expansion; and add each bypass as a fixture line in the refused list so the lint is tested against them.

findings.anchor: @test "verdict-derive: an envelope as the writer before cycle-126 shaped it (rejected_count and a singular rejected_sidecar, since #832) is pre-FR-2, and a sidecar git tracks with its committed bytes is history whatever a checkout's write order made its mtime — a row appended since is a later run's and counts (thirty-fifth run, e2a DISS-C-004)"
findings.trigger_anchor: [ "$status" -eq 0 ] || { echo "the pre-cycle-126 shape is not legacy: $output"; return 1; }
findings.cross_file_justification: The behaviour lives in the verdict-derive script (not in the diff), but this diff-touched test pins it: an envelope carrying `rejected_count: 2` and a singular `rejected_sidecar`, beside a sidecar holding two rejected rows and a feedback file with no triage section, must exit 0 with `consistent == true`.
findings.description: The gate decides whether to enforce the rejected-payload triage contract from keys in the envelope itself. Dropping `metadata.rejected_sidecars` / `rejected_summary` and writing the pre-cycle-126 keys instead downgrades the envelope to "legacy", and the only output is a warning ("predates the rejected-payload contract"). The sibling sidecar's rows are then skipped whenever the sidecar is older than the envelope or byte-identical to HEAD, both of which the same writer controls (`touch -t`, or committing the sidecar alongside). This is a schema-downgrade switch on a file produced by the party the gate is checking. It is inherent to a gate that reads producer-controlled files with no provenance, so the realistic impact is a careless or adversarial agent silently passing the triage requirement rather than a security boundary being crossed.
findings.failure_mode: A dissent run or a later edit writes the envelope in the pre-FR-2 shape (or the FR-2 keys are stripped during a merge); the feedback file omits the `## Rejected dissent payloads` section; verdict-derive exits 0 and the rejected payloads are never triaged, with only a warning that nothing in the pipeline fails on.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat the legacy shape as a violation (not a warning) when the envelope's own `model`/`status` or a `schema_enforced`/writer-version field proves it was produced after the FR-2 cut-over, or gate on the writer version recorded in the envelope rather than on key presence. At minimum, surface the legacy warning as a non-zero exit under a strict flag used in CI, and add a test asserting the strict path refuses this fixture.

findings.trigger_anchor: @test "verdict-derive: a fixture repository's git never acts on a caller's: under a hook's GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE or GIT_INDEX_FILE, _vd_git builds the fixture in its own directory and leaves the caller's repository as it was (thirty-ninth run, c2d DISS-C-001)"
findings.description: The isolation test for the fixture git helper only proves that GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE and GIT_INDEX_FILE from the caller's environment do not reach the fixture repository. The suite's own s35 test lists the rest of git's repository set as variables that must not decide anything (GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY, GIT_COMMON_DIR, GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES, GIT_NAMESPACE), but only for the script under test, never for `_vd_git`, which runs `init`, `add`, `commit` and `rm --cached`. If `_vd_git` scrubs only the three tested variables, a suite run inside a hook or a wrapper that exports GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY or GIT_COMMON_DIR would write fixture objects into the caller's object store, and with GIT_COMMON_DIR the fixture's `commit` would update `refs/heads/*` in the caller's repository. GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL / XDG_CONFIG_HOME are likewise unasserted, so a caller's `core.hooksPath` or `init.templateDir` could run hooks during the fixture commit.
findings.failure_mode: The suite is invoked from a git hook or CI wrapper that exports GIT_COMMON_DIR or GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY; fixture commits land in the caller's object store and, under GIT_COMMON_DIR, move the caller's branch ref to a fixture commit. The existing isolation test stays green because it never sets those variables.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the `gv` loop to GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY, GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES, GIT_COMMON_DIR, GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES, GIT_NAMESPACE, GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM and XDG_CONFIG_HOME, pointing each at the caller fixture, and assert `before == after` and that no new objects appear under the caller's `.git/objects`. In `_vd_git`, prefer `env -i PATH=… HOME=… GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1 GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null git -C "$1" …` over unsetting a list.

findings.anchor: .claude/skills/autonomous-agent/SKILL.md <input_guardrails> table row: `Script missing, non-zero exit, or unparseable output | Continue — fail-open`
findings.cross_file_justification: The diff commits, verbatim, a real dissenter finding that the autonomous skill continues when the guardrails orchestrator is missing, exits non-zero, or returns unparseable output. The new README goes further: it states that `guardrails-orchestrator.sh` passes `--mode run`, which the danger-level enforcer rejects, so run-mode input guardrails fall open. The README marks the bead (bd-rk9o, P2) as still open. The diff therefore documents a live bypass of a pre-execution security control without fixing it.
findings.description: Pre-existing and tracked, not introduced by this diff, but the diff's own README upgrades the dissenter's claim from 'an attacker who can trigger a validator error bypasses the guardrail' to 'the guardrail's own invocation is rejected by the enforcer on every run-mode call, so the fail-open branch is the normal path'. If that reading is correct, the input guardrail for a skill with write, execute, web, and agent-spawn capabilities effectively never evaluates the user prompt/args. The lead tallied this MEDIUM as 'pre-existing'; from an exploitability standpoint an always-skipped pre-execution policy check on an autonomous agent is a significant gap. I could not read SKILL.md, guardrails-orchestrator.sh, or the enforcer to confirm the deterministic mode mismatch; the evidence is the README text and the fixture payload shipped in this diff.
findings.failure_mode: Any invocation prompt, including an injected or policy-blocked one, reaches the privileged autonomous workflow (file writes, command execution, web access, sub-agent spawn) without the input guardrail ever evaluating it, because the orchestrator call is rejected (or otherwise errors) and the skill continues on the fail-open branch.
findings.suggested_fix: Fix the `--mode run` / enforcer mismatch so the orchestrator actually runs, and change the SKILL.md policy to fail closed on missing script, non-zero exit, or unparseable output (at most allow a narrowly scoped, explicitly approved infrastructure-outage override). Add a test that invokes guardrails-orchestrator.sh exactly as the skill does and asserts a non-zero/unparseable result halts the run. Until then, raise bd-rk9o above P2 and note in the fixture README that the bypass is deterministic, not attacker-triggered.

findings.trigger_anchor: tests/unit/adversarial-review-repair-loop.bats: `[ "$(_repair_model_chain "gpt-5.3-codex")" = "gpt-5.3-codex" ]` and the `process_findings ... "gpt-5.3-codex"` calls; tests/unit/adversarial-review-schema-enforced.bats FR7-9 grep-lock on `_adv_invoke_hop ... invoke_dissenter`
findings.cross_file_justification: The diff's tests pin the dissent/repair hop path (`_adv_invoke_hop` -> `_adv_with_cli_lock` -> `invoke_dissenter`) that sends system and user prompts to external models such as gpt-5.3-codex and gpt-5.5-pro via codex-headless. cheval's `filter_context` / trust_scopes `context_access` is the control that decides whether security findings, business-logic code, and architecture reach those models. The supplied P0 test file pins that this control fails open: an unknown provider/model, a model entry without `context_access`, or `None` trust scopes all resolve to DEFAULT_CONTEXT_ACCESS (all 'full').
findings.description: The context filter defaults to full access when the model is not found in model-permissions.yaml, when its entry predates v7 and lacks `context_access`, or when scopes are None. These are enshrined as expected behaviour by the tests. Combined with the diff adding new external model ids to the fallback/repair chains (gpt-5.3-codex, gpt-5.5-pro), any model id that lacks a permissions entry, or is mistyped, receives unredacted security audit content and code. Separately, `test_audit_returns_original_messages` pins that audit mode returns the original messages even for a model whose scopes say `security: none`; if audit mode is ever the production default, the filter is log-only. I could not read context_filter.py or model-permissions.yaml to confirm which models are registered or what the production mode is.
findings.failure_mode: A model added to a dissent or repair chain without a model-permissions.yaml entry (or with a pre-v7 entry) is sent full security findings, CVE details, secrets-adjacent error text, and business-logic source, defeating the epistemic trust boundary the filter exists to enforce.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the unknown-model and missing-`context_access` cases resolve to the most restrictive profile for non-native providers (or refuse the hop with a clear error), and keep the all-full default only for explicitly native-runtime providers. Add a test that loads the real model-permissions.yaml and asserts every model id referenced by adversarial-review.sh's chains has a `context_access` block. Assert that audit mode is opt-in and not the default in production.

findings.anchor: .claude/skills/autonomous-agent/resources/phase-mechanics.md Phase 0.0 case `*) # Other error - log and continue`

findings.cross_file_justification: The diff exercises external OpenAI-family reviewer hops. The only test that reads the real permissions entry for such a model (`openai/gpt-5.2`) wraps its assertion in `if scopes and "context_access" in scopes:`, so it passes vacuously if the block is removed; `test_gpt_reviewer_scopes` uses hand-built scopes, not the yaml.
findings.description: No test pins that the real model-permissions.yaml entry for an external reviewer actually restricts `security` to `none`. Deleting or renaming the `context_access` block for gpt-5.2 would make the filter fall open (see SEC-002) with the suite still green.

findings.anchor: tests/unit/adversarial-review-repair-loop.bats @test "C14: a repair OF the derived failure_mode (it failed validation) is the model's text — the derived marker is not carried onto it"
findings.description: The new test pins that when the repair model rewrites `failure_mode`, the result carries `failure_mode_derived: null`, i.e. it is indistinguishable from a failure_mode the dissenter wrote. Only the envelope-level `repaired_count` records that a repair happened; per-finding provenance of model-authored text is lost. Downstream consumers (verdict tallies, sidecars, humans triaging) treat repaired text as the dissenter's own evidence.
findings.failure_mode: A finding whose failure_mode was written by the repair model, not the dissenter, is reported and acted on as if the dissenter asserted it; a hallucinated or weakened failure statement cannot be traced back to the repair hop.
findings.suggested_fix: Set a per-field provenance marker (e.g. `failure_mode_repaired: true` / `repaired_fields: [...]`) when the repair model supplies the violated field, and keep it through to the verdict and sidecar.

findings.cross_file_justification: The diff introduces test coverage for the new per-binary CLI lock (`_adv_cli_lock_dir`, `_adv_with_cli_lock` in adversarial-review.sh) and shows the lock directory is `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/loa-headless-locks-<uid>`. The suites override XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, so nothing in the diff pins the behaviour when it is unset (CI, cron, containers).
findings.description: Hardening note; the fallback could not be verified from the diff. If `_adv_cli_lock_dir` falls back to a shared directory such as /tmp with the predictable name `loa-headless-locks-<uid>`, another local user can pre-create it (or a symlink) and either deny the lock permanently or redirect lock files. The tests themselves are hermetic and correct.
findings.failure_mode: With XDG_RUNTIME_DIR unset, the headless CLI lock lives in a world-writable predictable path; a local attacker pre-creates it and every *-headless dissent/repair hop fails or waits indefinitely.
findings.suggested_fix: When XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is unset, create the lock dir with `mkdir -m 0700` under a per-user location, verify it is a real directory owned by the current uid and not a symlink before use, and add a test that unsets XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and asserts the resolved path and its mode.

findings.description: `_dir_trustworthy` returns True as soon as the group-write bit is clear and only calls `_acl_extended` in the group-writable branch. That is sound for POSIX ACLs (group bits are the mask over named entries) but not for NFSv4 ACLs: the server synthesizes st_mode from OWNER@/GROUP@/EVERYONE@ only, so a named-user ACE granting write (the very `system.nfs4_acl` case the docstring cites) is invisible in the mode bits. A home directory or TMPDIR on such a mount is accepted as 'no other user can write' while another account can create entries above the isolated cwd.
findings.failure_mode: On an NFSv4-backed home or tmp, a second local account holding a named-user write ACE on an ancestor plants CLAUDE.md / .mcp.json / AGENTS.md above the headless cwd. The reviewer CLI loads it, giving that account prompt injection into the dissent voice and MCP server execution, which is the exact vector this module was written to close.
findings.suggested_fix: Call `_acl_extended(path)` on every ancestor regardless of the S_IWGRP bit (treat any `system.*acl*` xattr as untrusted unless parsed), or at minimum do so when the path is on a network filesystem. Keep the current fast-path only when `listxattr` reports no ACL names.

findings.cross_file_justification: The `name` argument is supplied by adapter subclasses outside this diff; if any of them derive it from the catalog `type`/cli identifier or an environment override, the value is operator- or repo-controlled rather than a constant.
findings.description: `private_workspace(name)` joins `name` onto the vetted base without checking it is a single path component. The ancestor-trust walk (`_chain_private`, `_project_marker`) runs on the base only, and the final `os.lstat` verifies owner and mode of the leaf but not of any ancestors that `name` introduces. A `name` containing `/` or `..` yields a 0700 directory under an unvetted ancestor that passes every check in the function.
findings.failure_mode: A value such as `../../tmp/x` relocates the 'private' cwd under world-writable `/tmp`, so any local user can again plant `/tmp/CLAUDE.md` on the CLI's discovery path. Exploitability depends on how callers build `name`; with a hard-coded constant the gap is latent.
findings.suggested_fix: Reject `name` unless `name == os.path.basename(name)` and it matches `^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$`, and assert `os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(path)) == base` after the mkdir before returning.

findings.description: `_TRUSTED_ABOVE` is a mutable module global in production code that, when non-None, short-circuits both `_chain_private` and `_project_marker` for the named root and every ancestor via `_trusted_stop`. Nothing restricts it to a test context and nothing logs when it is active, so a conftest leaking into a non-test import, a monkeypatch left behind, or future env plumbing silently disables the entire ancestor-trust and project-marker check.
findings.failure_mode: The isolation guarantee is turned off without any visible signal; an operator reading the diagnostics cannot tell that the headless cwd was never vetted.
findings.suggested_fix: Honour the hook only when an explicit test marker is present (e.g. `PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST` in the environment), emit a WARNING whenever it is non-None, or pass the trusted root as a function parameter from the tests instead of a module global.

findings.title: Untrusted review prompt is passed on argv and exposed to local users
findings.description: The agy adapter still places the full flattened review prompt in the process argument vector via `agy -p <prompt>`. The new comments explicitly acknowledge that argv is readable through `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and `ps` while the process runs. Review prompts commonly contain private diffs, source snippets, redacted-but-sensitive diagnostics, and occasionally secrets from the reviewed tree. On a shared host, any local user can race-read those arguments without needing access to the repository or Loa logs.
findings.impact: A malicious or compromised local account on the cheval host can steal prompt contents for every agy-backed Gemini review, including proprietary code and any credentials accidentally present in diffs. This is a direct cross-user information disclosure.
findings.recommendation: Do not dispatch agy with the prompt in argv. Re-probe whether `agy -p` can read from stdin, or add a secure prompt-file transport inside a 0700 private workspace if the CLI supports it. Until then, disable agy on shared hosts or route oversized/sensitive reviews to providers that use stdin or private prompt files.
findings.failure_mode: The agy adapter still places the full flattened review prompt in the process argument vector via `agy -p <prompt>`.

findings.cross_file_justification: The diff-touched agy adapter newly pins every hop to one stable cwd and passes it to run_subprocess_pgkill. The only defenses named in the new comments live in loa_cheval/providers/headless_cli.py (private_workspace's project-file check), which is imported by the diff but not shown, and in agy's --sandbox behaviour, which the comments state is 'not yet probed live'.
findings.description: The agy hop runs an agentic CLI with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` on untrusted content (the review diff is a prompt-injection vector) and, as of this change, does so inside a single persistent directory shared by every hop on the host. The previous per-hop directory bounded a hijacked hop's side effects to itself; a stable cwd turns any write the agent performs into state that every later hop inherits. The comments rest on two unverified claims: (a) `--sandbox` denies cwd writes (explicitly unprobed, and gemini-lineage sandboxes normally mount the project cwd read-write so the agent can edit it), and (b) `private_workspace` refuses a planted GEMINI.md or .gemini directory. Claim (b) cannot be verified from the diff and must cover everything a gemini-lineage CLI loads from cwd: `.gemini/settings.json` (which can declare `mcpServers` with arbitrary `command` entries and tooling/sandbox settings), `.env` and `.gemini/.env`, `GEMINI.md`, and `.geminiignore`. The sibling `loa-claude-ws` sits under the same base; if cwd writes are not denied, a relative write into `../loa-claude-ws/.claude/settings.json` (hooks) or `.mcp.json` carries from an agy hop into the next claude hop.
findings.failure_mode: A crafted diff under review prompt-injects the agy agent, which writes configuration or instruction files into the persistent workspace (or a sibling workspace). The next hop loads attacker-controlled settings: MCP server commands or hooks execute arbitrary code on the cheval host, or the reviewer's instructions are silently rewritten so later reviews approve malicious changes.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep agy disabled until the T4.1 re-probe demonstrates that `--sandbox` denies writes to the cwd and to its parent. Independently of that probe: make the stable workspace non-writable between hops (chmod 0500 after creation; the gemini project registry only needs the path to exist), have `private_workspace` fail closed when the directory contains any entry at all rather than a fixed denylist, and apply the same emptiness check to every sibling workspace before each hop. Add tests that plant `.gemini/settings.json`, `.env`, `GEMINI.md`, and `.claude/settings.json` in the base and assert the hop is refused.

findings.description: The agy adapter still places the entire flattened prompt (the review diff) as an argv element after `-p`. On Linux `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` is world-readable unless /proc is mounted with hidepid, so any local user can read the full prompt with `ps -o args` for the whole life of the hop, which can last up to the catalog timeout. The same change closes this exposure for claude-headless by moving its prompt to stdin, and the new module doc acknowledges agy's exposure remains open because stdin delivery for `-p` was never probed.
findings.failure_mode: Another local account on the cheval host reads the code under review, including any secrets, pre-release code, or customer data present in the diff, without any privilege beyond a shell on the same machine.
findings.suggested_fix: Probe `agy -p` with the prompt delivered on stdin via `input=` (communicate() writes then closes the pipe, so the later permission-prompt read still sees EOF). If agy accepts it, drop the positional prompt from argv as the claude adapter did. If agy cannot read the prompt from stdin, keep agy disabled on shared hosts or require /proc hidepid=2 as a documented deployment precondition.

findings.description: The grok staging-failure message previously reported only the exception class name, a deliberate redaction. The diff appends the full exception text, which for an OSError includes the absolute path of the private workspace base (for example a /run/user/<uid> or home-directory path that reveals the username). The agy adapter likewise interpolates the workspace path and `exc.filename` into its new vanished-cwd and exec-failure messages. These strings travel inside ProviderUnavailableError into the MODELINV ledger, chain diagnostics, and potentially the review output returned to the caller.
findings.failure_mode: Local filesystem layout, usernames, and runtime directory paths of the cheval host leak into logs and review artifacts that are shared more widely than the host itself.
findings.suggested_fix: Log the full exception at debug level and keep the operator-facing message to the errno name plus the basename of the offending path. If the full path is needed for triage, gate it behind an explicit verbose-diagnostics setting.

findings.cross_file_justification: The staleness rule and the hold mechanism live in loa_cheval/providers/headless_cli.py, which the diff imports but does not show. The ordering that opens the window is in the diff-touched grok adapter.
findings.description: The grok adapter now sweeps un-held workspaces under the shared private base, then creates its own directory, then takes the hold. The comment says a held workspace is 'never swept', implying the hold is the liveness marker. Two concurrent grok hops can interleave so that hop B's sweep runs after hop A's mkdtemp but before hop A's hold, in which case A's fresh directory looks stale and is removed. If the staleness rule has no age threshold, this is a reachable race under the default concurrency limit of 50 slots.
findings.failure_mode: A concurrent hop deletes another hop's fresh workspace; the victim hop's prompt write or spawn fails and is converted into a walkable ProviderUnavailableError, so the review diff is forwarded to the next provider in the chain, possibly a different vendor than the operator intended for that hop.
findings.suggested_fix: Create and hold the directory before sweeping, or have the sweep skip directories younger than a grace period (for example two minutes) in addition to skipping held ones. Add a test that interleaves two hops and asserts neither loses its workspace.

findings.description: The gemini adapter now injects GEMINI_SANDBOX=false into the child environment on every hop unless the operator's gemini_extra_flags ask for a sandbox. gemini-cli reads that variable ahead of both --sandbox and the user's settings.json tools.sandbox, so any sandbox the operator configured globally is suppressed for these hops. The adapter feeds untrusted review content to a CLI that still exposes read-only tools (file reads bounded in-process to the workspace, web fetch and search), and the project's own cursor adapter treats OS confinement as part of the hardening for exactly this threat. The override happens with no check for an ambient sandbox and no log line, so an operator who believes their global sandbox applies has no runtime signal that it does not.
findings.failure_mode: An operator relies on a globally configured gemini sandbox (GEMINI_SANDBOX=docker or tools.sandbox=true) to confine a CLI that processes attacker-authored diffs. The hop silently disables it. A tool-boundary bug or prompt-injected tool use in plan mode now runs against the host filesystem instead of a container, and nothing in the logs shows the sandbox was dropped.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the stdin prompt path but surface the trade-off: when the inherited environment carries a non-false GEMINI_SANDBOX, or settings.json sets tools.sandbox, log a WARNING that the hop is overriding it and why. Alternatively expose an explicit model-config knob (for example gemini_sandbox: keep) that accepts the argv exposure and routes through the existing warning-and-bound path, so the override is an operator decision rather than an implicit default.

findings.description: _asks_sandbox re-implements yargs boolean semantics (short-option groups, =value, following true/false literal, --no- negation, end-of-options) to decide whether to leave an operator sandbox active. When it returns True the adapter does not set GEMINI_SANDBOX=false, and a sandboxed gemini run folds the stdin prompt back into the sandbox child's argv, where any local user can read it through /proc/<pid>/cmdline. The adapter warns and bounds the prompt length, but the exposure itself is accepted. Any mismatch between this emulation and the real CLI parser (version drift in gemini-cli's option table, yargs config changes, tokens like --s or -s1 that yargs treats as the alias and this function ignores or misreads) either spuriously leaves the ambient sandbox enabled or drops the warning.
findings.failure_mode: gemini-cli changes how it registers the sandbox option, or an operator writes a flag form this emulation reads differently than yargs. The hop either keeps a sandbox the operator did not ask for, putting the review prompt on a world-readable argv, or disables one they did ask for.
findings.suggested_fix: Fail closed instead of emulating the parser: raise ConfigError when any token in gemini_extra_flags matches sandbox-shaped forms (-s, --sandbox*, --no-sandbox, short groups containing s), with the message explaining that a gemini sandbox puts the prompt on argv. If operator sandboxes must remain supported, gate them behind an explicit config key and keep GEMINI_SANDBOX pinned (true or false) by the adapter so the outcome never depends on reproducing yargs.

findings.description: Two codex error messages now interpolate the raw exception: the workspace-creation failure (`failed to create isolated workspace: {type}: {exc}`) and the new OSError branch in _raise_spawn_error (`spawn failed ... {exc}`). For OSError the str() includes the filename argument, which here is the private workspace path under $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR or ~/.cache/loa, or the resolved CLI binary path. ProviderUnavailableError text is walkable and tends to be logged or written into review artifacts shared beyond the host.
findings.failure_mode: A hop fails on a developer or CI host and the error, carrying the local home-directory path and username, is written into a committed review report or a shared log stream.
findings.suggested_fix: Include errno and strerror rather than the full str(exc) (for example `{type(exc).__name__}: {exc.strerror or exc}` with the filename omitted), or route the path through the existing logger at DEBUG and keep the raised message path-free.

findings.description: In the cursor adapter, tempfile.mkdtemp runs and then hold_hop_workspace(workspace) is called before the try block that owns cleanup. If the lock acquisition raises (flock unsupported on the base filesystem, EMFILE, or any OSError), the freshly created workspace is never removed by this hop and persists until a later hop's one-day sweep. The codex adapter places the same call inside its try and does clean up. The leaked directory is empty for cursor, so this is a hygiene gap rather than data exposure, but it is an inconsistency in the new cleanup contract.
findings.failure_mode: On a filesystem where directory flock fails, every cursor hop leaks one empty 0700 directory under the private base; over a day of heavy use the base fills with entries the sweep then has to remove.
findings.suggested_fix: Move hold_hop_workspace into the try block (as codex does) or wrap it so that on failure the workspace is rmtree'd before the exception propagates.

findings.title: Agy/Gemini prompts can be exposed through process argv
findings.description: The change leaves at least one headless adapter path sending the review prompt on argv: the changelog states agy's prompt is still on argv by default, and Gemini returns to argv when sandbox flags are used. Review prompts include diffs and may contain credentials or proprietary code, so any local process able to read /proc/<pid>/cmdline can capture them during execution. This is a direct secrets exposure path; warnings and size caps do not remove the leak. Pass all prompts through stdin or a private 0600 file descriptor, and reject configurations that force argv transport.

findings.description: The sprint-248 notes state that claude, gemini (unsandboxed), codex, cursor and grok headless hops now receive the prompt on stdin or a private prompt file because an argv prompt is readable through `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. findings.description: In .loa.config.yaml, flatline_protocol.models.primary (was `opus`) and run_bridge models[0].model_id (was `claude-opus-5`) are switched to `claude-headless`. The previous http_api ids failed INVALID_CONFIG without ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, i.e. fail-closed. The new CLI-backed entry resolves its binary, auth route, and billed account from CLAUDE_HEADLESS_BIN at runtime. The diff's own comments state that a shell without that variable (cron, CI, a fresh login) silently runs Flatline and Bridgebuilder hops, which carry repo source and diffs, on the plain claude CLI's consumer login rather than the Bedrock route the 2026-10-01 operator directive requires. Nothing in the config or the envelope pins, verifies, or records the route actually taken. This is the KF-016 class (Bedrock-only operators silently degrading to another route) re-introduced for two more consumers, plus the KF-020 per-token billing exposure on the consumer plan. Verified from the diff text and comments only; the cheval adapter code was not readable in this audit.
findings.failure_mode: Unattended runs (spiral harness, CI, cron) send repository content through an unintended account and provider route outside the operator's Bedrock compliance boundary, with no error, no degraded marker, and no envelope field that distinguishes the route; spend lands on a personal subscription.
findings.suggested_fix: Fail closed again: have the headless adapter refuse to start when providers.bedrock.compliance_profile demands Bedrock and CLAUDE_HEADLESS_BIN is unset, or declare the wrapper path in the model catalog entry instead of the environment. Record the resolved binary and route in the MODELINV row and the adversarial/Flatline envelope. findings.anchor: A re-review or re-audit adds its round's label and `br label add` never removes the other
findings.description: The new .claude/skills/auditing-security/resources/BEADS-WORKFLOW.md (and the mirrored reviewing-code copy) instructs adding exactly one of `security-approved` / `security-blocked` per round but explicitly never removes the prior round's label, so a task blocked in round 2 still carries `security-approved` from round 1. The doc declares the latest free-text `SECURITY AUDIT:` comment to be the verdict of record, but comments are not machine-queryable; labels are the only structured state, and the sibling reviewing-code doc titles its table 'Using Labels for Status'. Any consumer that filters on label presence (br list --label, a merge/ready gate, the autonomous harness) will read a stale approval. The flushed JSONL is committed, so the stale approval persists in history.
findings.failure_mode: A sprint whose most recent security audit verdict is CHANGES_REQUIRED passes any label-based gate as security-approved; downstream automation or a human skimming labels proceeds to merge on a superseded approval.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the labels mutually exclusive: run `br label remove <task-id> security-approved` before `br label add <task-id> security-blocked` (and vice versa), or use round-scoped labels (security-approved-r2) and have gates read the COMPLETED marker / verdict-derive.sh output rather than label presence. Update both BEADS-WORKFLOW.md files so 'exactly one of' is actually true after a re-audit.

findings.description: The updated row in .claude/rules/skill-invariants.md enumerates every Bash use these two skills need: adversarial-review.sh, the verdict check, and qmd-context-query.sh. None is a git mutation, yet their disallowed-tools remains `NotebookEdit` alone, while the adjacent report-authoring row mechanically removes `Bash(git add/commit/push *)` as 'implementation-only git mutations'. The doc itself says disallowed-tools is 'a harness-level barrier that instructions cannot override' whereas zones are prose. reviewing-code and auditing-security are the skills most exposed to untrusted input: they read the diff under review and forward it to models, so a prompt injection embedded in reviewed code or comments reaches an agent that can still Write and run `git add/commit/push`.
findings.failure_mode: An injected instruction in a reviewed PR causes the review or audit agent to commit and push altered feedback files, ledgers, checkmarks, or application code; C-PROC-001 is enforced only by prose for exactly the skills that process adversarial content.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `Bash(git add/commit/push *)` to disallowed-tools for reviewing-code and auditing-security to match red-teaming and bridgebuilder-review, and extend validate-skill-capabilities.sh to WARN on any role: review skill that keeps git mutations. If a commit is required after `br sync --flush-only`, perform it in the orchestrator or a pre-commit hook rather than inside the review skill.

findings.anchor: single-voice: its companion is refused by the open breaker, the envelope reads companion_voice.status failed (not degraded)
findings.cross_file_justification: Before this diff Flatline's primary was the http_api id `opus` and Bridgebuilder's was `claude-opus-5`, so neither shared a circuit-breaker bucket with adversarial-review.sh's claude-headless companion. The .loa.config.yaml change places all three on anthropic/headless. grimoires/loa/known-failures.md KF-038 (added in this diff) documents the consequence: a companion refused by the open breaker yields companion_voice.status failed with degraded false and status clean/reviewed, and nothing in the unattended harness re-runs it; verdict-derive.sh (per sprint.md's amended criterion) does not refuse such an envelope.
findings.description: Switching Flatline and Bridgebuilder primaries to `claude-headless` puts them on the same anthropic/headless circuit breaker as the adversarial-review companion voice. The .loa.config.yaml comment added in this diff states that a Flatline rate limit opens that breaker for both, and the security audit that follows then runs single-voice: the companion is refused, the envelope reports companion_voice.status failed with degraded false, and the status remains clean or reviewed. KF-038 confirms this is the designed behaviour and that the unattended harness never re-runs the chunk. The audit gate therefore fails open to reduced coverage whenever a preceding phase on the same account trips the shared breaker, with no envelope field that an automated consumer treats as a failure signal.
findings.failure_mode: In the spiral harness a security audit that follows a Flatline phase on the same account records a clean or reviewed verdict with degraded:false while only the primary voice ran; the gate passes on halved coverage and no field an unattended consumer checks flags it. Anyone able to drive claude -p load on the host or exhaust the plan window can force the audit into single-voice mode.
findings.suggested_fix: Mark companion failure_class quota/model_unavailable/timeout as degraded:true in the envelope, or have verdict-derive.sh refuse an approval when voices_succeeded < voices_planned unless an explicit single-voice override is recorded in the feedback file. findings.description: The new Unicode gate in gh_anchor refuses categories No, Cf and Cn but admits Cc and Zl/Zp. san1 (the only sanitizer the title passes through) strips C0 control bytes and flattens \t \n \r, but it works on bytes under LC_ALL=C and never sees Unicode line terminators or C1 controls: NEL U+0085 (Cc), LINE SEPARATOR U+2028 (Zl), PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR U+2029 (Zp) and U+0080–U+009F (Cc) all survive into the heading line written by op_new and into the log/die messages that echo the title. Because `word()` returns false for these, the anchor is unaffected and the writer's own grep/awk/`\n`-based checks (duplicate check, next_kf_id, verify_and_swap's drop guard) see one physical line, so the write succeeds. Any consumer that splits on Unicode line boundaries (Python str.splitlines(), Java BufferedReader, many editors) sees `## KF-003: foo<U+2028>## KF-999: fake` as two headings, so a caller can smuggle a phantom `## KF-NNN:` heading or `| [KF-NNN](#…) |` Index row into such a reader while the shell-side integrity checks stay green. C1 controls (e.g. U+009B CSI, U+009D OSC) additionally reach the operator's terminal via `log`/`die` on xterm-class terminals that honour UTF-8-encoded C1.
findings.failure_mode: The single-line / control-free invariant that san1 is meant to enforce is ASCII-only; the new Unicode category filter was the natural place to close that gap and does not. A crafted --title injects extra logical lines for Unicode-aware readers of known-failures.md and can carry terminal control sequences into stderr output.
findings.suggested_fix: In the python3 gate, also exit 4 (or strip) for any c with unicodedata.category(c) in ("Cc", "Zl", "Zp") — this covers U+0085 and U+0080–U+009F as well as U+2028/U+2029 — and apply the same check to the ASCII/byte path by routing every non-ASCII title through python3 before the C1 bytes can be echoed. Alternatively extend san1 to delete the UTF-8 byte sequences \xC2[\x80-\x9F], \xE2\x80\xA8 and \xE2\x80\xA9.
